deep_why: The core challenge is predicting user behavior from timestamped events while respecting the hidden structure encoded in who-interacts-with-whom connections. Self-supervised learning works by teaching a model to predict the next step in a sequence reliably, establishing a sound foundation for reasoning about temporal patterns. But sequences alone cannot explain why some users behave similarly to others or why certain items cluster together; that relational structure lives in the interaction graph itself. By explicitly feeding graph-based relationship information into the event model, the method ensures the system learns both when things happen and how they connect through the underlying social and item topology. This two-fold view—temporal order plus relational structure—creates a richer signal that lets the model generalize better to unseen users and items, especially when behavioral data is sparse.

The core task is distinguishing answers written by machines from those written by people. This matters because it reveals whether a platform's value comes from human knowledge-sharing or from automated summaries passing as personal expertise. The method builds an ensemble of independent detection signals—each trained to spot a different telltale machine characteristic like unusual word variety, punctuation rhythm, or sentence structure. When multiple independent detectors agree, their combined opinion becomes far more trustworthy than any single judge, because machines tend to show consistent statistical quirks while human writing is more variable. This voting principle works because machine-generated text, trained on statistical patterns, produces measurable deviations from the messier distribution of authentic human communication. By stacking detectors, the ensemble amplifies true signals and dilutes random false alarms, achieving the reported 99.87% accuracy.

The core problem is that a general-purpose time-series forecaster outputs continuous numbers for rainfall, but real rainfall is fundamentally different: it is almost entirely zero (dry days) with occasional wet bursts of varying intensity. The mismatch between what the model naturally produces and what the data's true structure demands creates systematic errors—false drizzle alerts, missed extremes, miscalibrated intensities. The proposed wrapper corrects this by applying three mathematical truths: first, it restores the correct proportion of zero predictions using observed rain occurrence rates; second, it rescales the nonzero predictions to match the actual distribution of rainy-day intensities via a mathematical transform that preserves ordering; and third, it handles rare extreme rainfall via a specialist distribution designed for tail behavior. These corrections restore fidelity without retraining the model because they apply statistical facts about the data itself, independent of how the underlying forecaster was built.

The core challenge is learning from graphs that evolve over time, where new node types appear and visual styles shift, forcing a model to simultaneously learn new classes and forget old ones without collapsing its earlier knowledge. The method disentangles node representations into two separate channels: semantic factors that carry the class-identity signal, and style factors that capture the surface appearance variations caused by changing feature styles or edges. This separation works because it isolates what must transfer across time (the decision boundary for classification) from what changes (cosmetic visual patterns). By freezing one channel while updating another, and by replaying remembered examples from early tasks, the model can absorb new information without overwriting previous patterns. This structured forgetting—keeping semantics stable while letting style adjust—is mathematically sounder than monolithic retraining because it explicitly names and controls where catastrophic interference occurs.

This is a workshop announcement framing emerging challenges in digital advertising. The underlying tension is reconciling three conflicting goals: showing users relevant ads, protecting their privacy, and enabling advertisers to measure success. No deep mathematical explanation applies to an agenda-setting forum, but the problems it flags—balancing user choice against business incentives, deploying privacy-preserving measures without sacrificing targeting quality—are genuine research frontiers where formal reasoning, user studies, and empirical testing all contribute to finding sound solutions.

The core task is ranking short videos when user-interaction data is scarce (long-tail queries see few clicks), so counting clicks directly misleads. The method uses an LLM's world knowledge to estimate inherent video quality without relying on sparse user signals. This works because LLMs have absorbed patterns about what makes content valuable and credible from their training corpus. The framework then trains a smaller model to predict the LLM's quality judgments using video content features, and refines it via pairwise preference learning—teaching it to rank two videos correctly relative to each other, a task far easier than predicting absolute scores. At deployment, this learned model scores unseen videos quickly, promoting underexposed high-quality content. The soundness lies in bootstrapping quality judgment from external knowledge and then distilling it into a learnable model, breaking the dependency on sparse behavioral feedback.

Segmenting histopathology images using only image-level labels (not pixel-level truth) is hard because classes appear similar (inter-class homogeneity) and images of the same class look different (intra-class variation). The method constructs text descriptions for each category at multiple levels of specificity and trains the model to align visual features from different layers of the image encoder to these text descriptions. This works because text prompts create a stable, semantic anchor outside the visual domain—words like 'benign tissue' carry consistent meaning regardless of staining variation. By hierarchically organizing these prompts (whole-class prompts and sub-class prompts), the model learns to separate what is truly diagnostic from what is mere visual noise. The contrastive alignment principle ensures that visual and textual representations of the same concept pull together while mismatches repel, gradually sharpening the boundary between classes despite sparse labels.

The core observation is that conversational AI systems now autonomously create and store summaries of user conversations as 'memory,' building profiles of users without explicit permission. Understanding this requires examining what these memories contain and how they were formed. The analysis reveals that 96% are system-generated unilaterally, half contain psychological inferences, and most faithfully represent the conversation. The contribution is not mathematical but empirical and ethical: measuring where agency lies and what personal data is encoded in algorithmic memory. The Attribution Shield framework responds by training the model to anticipate sensitive inferences and alert users, a control-feedback loop that respects the mathematical principle that most harms from data processing stem from asymmetric information—users don't know what the system learned about them, so making predictions visible restores some symmetry.

Complex questions requiring multiple hops through a knowledge base are hard because each retrieval step introduces errors that compound, and poor question decomposition leads the search down dead ends. The method structures the problem as a reasoning tree where the original question is split into linked subqueries, with explicit entity tracking to distinguish what is given, what is known, and what must be found. This works because a tree representation forces logical clarity: each branch must connect to its parent, cycles are impossible, and the traversal order is explicit. By building a consensus tree (selecting the best decomposition from multiple candidates) and then traversing bottom-up while refining queries at each step, the method minimizes both decomposition errors and propagation of early mistakes. The tree structure itself is a mathematical guarantee that reasoning remains coherent—you cannot follow a malformed path because the structure forbids it.

Mobile video streaming requires ultra-low latency and packet loss recovery, and the standard approach applies Forward Error Correction equally to each frame. However, packet loss often comes in bursts that, while severe within a single frame, can be averaged out across a few frames because video is temporally smooth—humans tolerate a momentary glitch if the next frame arrives on time. The method expands the protection boundary from one frame to multiple frames, allowing the error correction to spread redundancy across time. This works because burst loss within a multi-frame window is statistically less concentrated than frame-level loss; spreading redundancy across more packets makes correction more efficient. The adaptive element continuously adjusts this boundary based on current network loss patterns and video bitrate, ensuring that redundancy investment matches the observed risk. This temporal pooling of error correction is mathematically sound because it exploits correlation in network conditions across successive frames.

Pixel tracking—invisible embedded images that leak user browsing to third-party servers—is hard to detect using rules or surface features because trackers use common infrastructure (CDNs, ad networks) that legitimate services also use. The method formulates detection as identifying which cross-site associations are tracking-related by constructing a directed graph where nodes are websites and edges represent HTTP traffic patterns. By encoding traffic into structured tuples and learning both semantic content and interaction patterns, the system can spot the correlations that distinguish genuine tracking from benign multi-site hosting. To overcome label scarcity, it uses an LLM with minimal expert guidance to auto-generate labels, bootstrapping a training set. The soundness here is that tracking leaves structural fingerprints in who talks to whom across sites; by explicitly modeling that structure and letting the system learn what patterns matter, detection becomes feasible without manual feature engineering.

Online advertising budgets must be spent smoothly across time to match campaign goals, but auctions are dynamic and bids fluctuate, making simple fixed-rate spending unstable. Control theory offers a principled solution: measure the current spend rate, compare it to the target rate, and adjust future bids proportionally. The method combines this feedback rule with hysteresis (a dead zone) to prevent oscillation caused by noise in the measurement. This works because proportional feedback is mathematically guaranteed to drive the system toward equilibrium when tuned correctly; hysteresis prevents the controller from overreacting to small random fluctuations. By carefully analyzing how to set the feedback gain and dead zone width, the approach ensures stable convergence to desired spend rates. This control-theoretic principle is sound because it is agnostic to the specific auction mechanics—it only requires that higher bids generally lead to higher spend, a universal property of online auctions.

Teaching a student knowledge model from one discipline must work across different subjects because core cognitive skills (memorization, understanding, reasoning) generalize, but the specific knowledge structure and terminology differ widely. The method separates student ability from subject content by using a cross-disciplinary graph to identify meta-skills—patterns in how students learn that persist across domains—and aligning these patterns across subjects. Simultaneously, a pre-trained language model extracts semantic relationships from course materials, surfacing conceptual connections that transcend terminology differences. This two-pronged approach works because human learning has both universal properties (how memory fades, how mastery compounds) and domain-specific properties (what concepts are foundational in math versus biology). By explicitly extracting and aligning the universal aspects while incorporating domain semantics, the model learns to transfer the former while respecting the latter, achieving the reported 14% improvement in accuracy across subjects.

Recommendation systems using graph neural networks suffer when random edge perturbations are used to generate training views, because removing real edges can destroy important signals (what users actually bought together), undermining the contrastive learning objective. The method proposes two complementary strategies: a generative model to construct new plausible graph structure capturing global patterns, and a denoising model to refine existing edges by suppressing likely false positives. This works because generative views preserve semantic structure while being statistically different from the original, and denoising removes noise rather than erasing signal. By using asymmetric contrastive learning—where negative samples are globally informed rather than purely local—and diffusion-guided refinement (progressive noise injection and recovery), the system learns robust representations even when data is sparse and noisy. The principle is that augmentations should modify the graph in semantically meaningful ways, not arbitrarily, so that the learned patterns reflect real collaborative patterns rather than artifacts of random corruption.

Sequential recommendation learns user preferences from the order of past interactions, but standard data augmentation techniques like random dropout or noise injection can obscure user intent by destroying meaningful patterns. The method proposes learnable perturbation and restoration networks that adaptively corrupt and repair user sequences in a semantically consistent manner. This works because it bypasses the assumption that all corruption strategies are equally valid; instead, the model learns what kinds of sequence changes preserve user intent and what changes constitute true augmentation. The contrastive learning objective then teaches the model that two semantically similar sequences should produce similar preference predictions while dissimilar sequences diverge. By automating augmentation selection, the approach ensures that positive examples in the contrastive pair are actually related to the same user intent, not just similar by accident. This adaptive principle is sounder than fixed augmentation because it lets the model discover which distortions reveal robust patterns versus which destroy real signal.
